source.title: Auditing Language Model Unlearning via Information Decomposition
source.authors: Anmol Goel; Alan Ritter; Iryna Gurevych

page_placements.theme: Weight and representation diagnostics that predict relearning vulnerability

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether unlearning leaves information about forgotten data in model representations, using linear probes and a PID-based audit rather than the claim's specified recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports representation-probe results, residual and unlearned knowledge scores, and correlations with attack success rates. It says it applies fine-tuning and refusal-direction ablation attacks, but reports correlations rather than attack-specific recovery outcomes. Forget Quality and abstention results do not establish the full claim version A, which also requires preserved general ability and attack outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study probes and decomposes representation-level information about the forget set after five approximate unlearning methods on TOFU and MUSE. It compares against a retrained-from-scratch control. This bears on the 'blocks access rather than deletes' part of version C. It does not report recovery rates from the fine-tuning or direction-ablation attacks it ran; it reports only correlations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that approximate unlearning is shallow: membership information about the forget set stays linearly decodable and redundant with the base model despite output metrics like Forget Quality. Gradient-based methods leave the most; RMU and NPO are comparatively effective. Residual knowledge correlates with attack success, and a residual-risk abstention score improves forget quality at small utility cost.
record.recipe_differences: This study introduces a representation-level PID audit and probes existing unlearning methods; it does not reproduce the original methods' recovery-attack evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Residual Knowledge differs by unlearning method and model family; the paper also reports consistent relative trends for smaller models and a separate MUSE evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual knowledge, the PID redundancy of membership information, correlates positively (0.45 to 0.71) with attack success rates for fine-tuning and orthogonalization attacks. MIA correlates more weakly (0.24 to 0.51). The ASRs themselves are not given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-level residual membership information predicts vulnerability of unlearned models to relearning and direction-ablation attacks.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper says its neural information estimator provides a lower bound on the true information quantities. It studies English-language unlearning of fine-tuned LLMs and does not provide certified guarantees. The Figure 2 probe curves are figure-only, with no curve values stated in the text; Table 2 reports correlations rather than attack recovery rates.
record.rows_left_out: No reported residual-knowledge rows were left out. Figure 2 is represented by one figure-only row for each plotted method, rather than separate rows for every layer; the text does not state the individual curve values.

untested.parts: Neither near-chance targeted accuracy nor preserved general ability is tested jointly with attack failure. Forget Quality is reported, but utility is explicitly set aside.
A benign fine-tuning attack (from Łucki et al.) was run, but no recovered-accuracy or ASR values are reported; only regression coefficients are given.
Refusal-direction ablation was run, but its recovery rates are not reported. Only the representation-persistence part of C is tested.
No prompting, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
No method is claimed or tested as robust to recovery attacks; the abstention defense is inference-time mitigation.

missing.what: Forget Quality per method and model (e.g. llama GA 0.55, RMU 0.72), which shows the output-level 'apparent success' that the residual knowledge is contrasted with. Unlearned Knowledge values are also unrecorded.
Attack success rates for the Łucki et al. fine-tuning and refusal-direction ablation attacks. They were run but are not reported anywhere in the text, so they cannot be rows.

record.verdict_notes: The measure is membership information (forget vs retain), not recall of forgotten facts, so the link to C is to its 'blocks access rather than deleting' analysis. Figure 2 has no control probe curve, and its model is llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Table 2 significance markers are unusual (* p<0.01, ** p<0.05), and the regression uses ASR as predictor of residual knowledge. The retrained control appears only for TOFU 7B to 9B (Table 1). None of the original sources is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Does not jointly test near-chance targeted-knowledge performance, preserved general ability, and whether simple attacks fail to recover knowledge.
The paper applies a fine-tuning attack but does not report how much knowledge it restores; it reports correlations with residual knowledge.
Does not test whether ablating an activation direction restores knowledge. It tests whether forgotten-data information remains decodable from representations after unlearning.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context-information recovery attack is tested.
The paper does not test whether a method resists the specified recovery attacks.
